title: Two-Word Concatenation Check
hints: if target = left + right, both left and right individually need to be present in the word list - what's the fastest way to check 'is this string in my set of words' as you scan through target?
insert every word into a trie so that checking membership of any prefix is fast, character by character
walk target from the beginning, one character at a time, following the trie; every time you land on a node marked end-of-word, you've found a valid 'left' piece - note that position
for each such split position, check whether the remaining suffix of target (from that position to the end) is itself a complete word by walking the trie again from the root
remember the 'two different entries' rule: if left and right are equal in text, you need that word to appear in the list at least twice - track insertion counts per word, not just presence
commonMistakes: allowing a single list entry to be used for both halves when the word only appears once in the list
checking only one split point (e.g. the midpoint) instead of trying every valid prefix/suffix split
confusing this with 'any number of words' (like Word Break) instead of exactly two

content.problemStatement:
You're given a space-delimited string of lowercase `words` and a separate `target` word.

**Determine whether `target` can be formed by concatenating exactly two different entries from the word list, in some order, and return true if so, false otherwise.**

Each entry may only be used once; if the same word text appears twice in the list, that counts as two separate usable entries.
constraints: target and all words consist only of lowercase English letters
notes: target can only be formed by using the same list entry twice (not allowed unless it appears twice)
target's split point could occur at more than one position; only one needs to work
no combination of any two entries forms target

sampleTestCases.explanation: "cats" + "dog" = "catsdog", and both are separate entries in the list
"a" + "a" would require two entries equal to "a", but the list only has one
the list has "a" twice, as two separate entries, so "a" + "a" is valid

optimal.time: O(len(target)) per split check using the trie, O(total word characters) to build
optimal.pattern: insert all words into a trie, then walk target from the start following trie edges; every position where you land on an end-of-word node is a candidate split point - check whether the remaining suffix is also a complete word in the trie (using a duplicate-count trie so reusing the same text twice is allowed only if it was inserted twice)

bruteForce.approach: put word counts in a frequency map; for every split point of target into a left and right part, check both parts exist in the map with enough remaining count
bruteForce.time: O(len(target) * average lookup cost), simple but requires careful counting to respect 'two different entries'
